title: Latency Chronicles: time-budget tuning for continuous inference
content:
Purpose:
This is a working log describing a set of targeted experiments aimed at tuning the time-budget (timeout) and implicit per-request time allocation inside the continuous inference scheduler. Goal: reduce 99th/99.9th latency tail without sacrificing multi-tenant fairness or steady-state throughput.

Context / motivation:
We see recurring spikes in 99.9th latency for bursty traffic patterns (short, high-QPS bursts from testbed workloads), particularly when requests of heterogeneous token lengths are mixed. Continuous batching is great for average cost reduction but the current flush/time-budget heuristics create outlier climbs under microbursts. We want to characterize if we can: (1) reallocate a small explicit time budget per-slot (timelock) to reduce stragglers, (2) keep batch sizes high for throughput, and (3) preserve fairness across tenants.

Experiment summary (high level):
- Platform: dedicated GPU pool (A100-80GB), 4x worker shards, runtime v1.18.
- Workload: synthetic mixed-token generator (uniform short 8-16 tokens at 60% of traffic, long 512-1024 tokens at 40%). Burst profile: 100 qps sustained with 500 qps 2s spikes every 60s.
- Metric focus: P50/P95/P99/P99.9 latency per request end-to-end (queue+inference), tokens/sec throughput, wasted-prefill-percent, fairness index (Jain) among 6 tenants.
- Vars: global time-budget (tb_global) that controls maximum wallclock wait for batch formation; per-slot timelock (slot_timelock) that triggers partial flush of the slot if certain tokens are still pending; permissive prefill threshold (prefill_pct) that determines when we prefill KV caches and start early compute.

Bench harness and tracing:
- Replayed production traces (sanitized) via replay-runner v0.9. Command used: 
  ./replay-runner --trace traces/sanitized/microbursts-2025-01-23.json --concurrency 16 --target 4-workers --trace-mode mixed-sized
- Microtraces collected with microtrace-id annotation and exported to tracer-stack for visualization (span names: queue.wait, slot.open, prefill.start, kernel.exec, kv.fetch).
- Light sampling profiler enabled at 1% to keep overhead low.

Baseline (control):
- tb_global=35ms, slot_timelock disabled, prefill_pct=0.6. Observed:
  - P50: 18ms, P95: 78ms, P99: 210ms, P99.9: 1280ms.
  - Tokens/sec steady-state: 45k/sec per shard.
  - Wasted prefill percent: 3.4% (prefill started but batch shrank).
  - Jain fairness index: 0.88 (some demotion of long requests during bursts).
  - Observation: long requests accumulate inside active slots and trigger big kernels late in timeline, causing head-of-line (HOL) amplification for other slots due to GPU preemption and KV cache thrash.

Experiment A — aggressive global time-budget shrink:
- Set tb_global = 18ms. Keep other knobs default.
- Result:
  - P50: 20ms, P95: 90ms, P99: 300ms, P99.9: 760ms.
  - Tokens/sec: -8% throughput drop vs baseline.
  - Wasted prefill percent: 7.1% (more early flushes).
  - Fairness: 0.92 (slight improvement).
- Interpretation: Lower tb reduces long tail but increases wasted prefill and reduces throughput. Better fairness because long requests less likely to hold slots open. Tradeoff: throughput cost ~8%.

Experiment B — bounded per-slot timelock + permissive prefill:
- slot_timelock=30ms, tb_global=35ms, prefill_pct=0.5 (start earlier).
- Mechanism: each slot keeps a per-slot backstop timer; once timelock fires, the scheduler assembles a partial batch from the slot’s ready requests and flushes to avoid head-of-line long requests blocking small ones in other slots. Prefill earlier to avoid kernel overhead at flush time.
- Result:
  - P50: 19ms, P95: 75ms, P99: 220ms, P99.9: 400ms.
  - Tokens/sec: -2% throughput.
  - Wasted prefill percent: 4.9%.
  - Fairness: 0.95.
- Interpretation: Per-slot timelock converges to much better tail (almost 3x improvement at P99.9) while preserving throughput. Prefill earlier smoothed kernel start costs and reduced variance.

Experiment C — adaptive timelock based on slot occupancy and request-length histogram:
- slot_timelock = if (slot_occupancy >= 0.7*max_slot) then 18ms else 45ms; tb_global=35ms; prefill_pct=0.55.
- Idea: if a slot is filling rapidly, use smaller timelock to let it flush while others keep filling; for sparse slots give longer timelock to avoid needless flushes.
- Result:
  - P50: 17ms, P95: 72ms, P99: 195ms, P99.9: 420ms.
  - Tokens/sec: +1% (small improvement via better alignment of flushes to natural microbursts).
  - Wasted prefill: 3.8%.
  - Fairness: 0.94.
- Interpretation: adaptive timelock helps align flushes with slot-level dynamics, slightly improves throughput and keeps tail latency low.

Profiling insights and hotspots:
- Kernel exec variance: long requests produced a small set of very heavy kernels (~0.8% of kernels) that occupied the GPU for >600ms; these were the primary cause of 99.9s when they coincided with flushes of multiple slots.
- KV cache pressure: when prefill_pct was low, we saw more repeated KV fetches and cache churn; early prefill at moderate levels (0.5-0.6) amortized KV setup cost and reduced kernel variance.
- Queue micro-serialization: large request serialization into big kernels caused driver-side serialization spikes (nvml queues observed spikes aligning with P99 events).
- Prefill wastage correlated strongly with small time-budget values; wasted prefill cost is not free but lower than paying 800ms P99.9 penalties.

Operational considerations:
- Multi-tenant fairness: per-slot timelock improves fairness index because small requests get early partial flush opportunities. Need to verify under tenant weight skews (one noisy tenant sending all long requests).
- SLOs and rollout plan: recommend canary rollout behind canary routing with 5% traffic, monitor P99.9, error budget burn, and throughput. If P99.9 improves without >5% throughput regression, expand.
- Telemetry additions: add histograms of slot_timelock firing frequency, per-slot occupancy distribution, and kernel-duration percentiles per model-variant. Create derived metric: slot_flush_cause{timelock|timeout|capacity}.

Open questions / next probes:
1) How does adaptive timelock interact with KV cache prewarming for long-context models? Need runs with 1k/2k context models.
2) Should timelock be tenant-aware (weight lower-priority tenants to longer timelocks)? Run tenancy-skew tests.
3) Can we reduce wasted prefill overhead by lazy prefill (start prefill only if slot reaches N requests OR if oldest-request-age > X ms)?
4) Cost modeling: quantify token cost impact vs latency improvement for hosted vs dedicated customers.

Immediate next steps (action items):
- [Maya] Create canary PR implementing slot_timelock + metrics (PR draft: linked).
- [Jonah] Add slot-level histograms to observability dashboards (dash id: ENG-SRV-356).
- [Priya] Run tenancy-skew simulation next week (private run).
- [Ethan] Prepare confluence write-up and include per-tenant SLO guidance.

Notes to self (rough):
- When writing tests, include microtrace-case where two long requests are interleaved with many short ones; verify partial flush does not cause replay inconsistencies.
- Keep sampling profiler at 1% for CI; higher rates skew scheduling behavior.

Appendix: quick command snippets and parameter grid used
- Grid: tb_global in {18, 25, 35}, slot_timelock in {disabled, 18, 30, adaptive}, prefill_pct in {0.45,0.5,0.55,0.6}
- Replay command: ./replay-runner --workers 4 --profile 1% --params tb_global=18,slot_timelock=30,prefill_pct=0.5 --outdir runs/2025-02-24
